title: Jerusalem Through Time
subtitle: Topography, archaeology, and period-aware interpretation
summary: Explore Jerusalem's southeastern ridge, Temple Mount precinct, water systems, valleys, and eastern ridge across major biblical and Second Temple periods without turning reconstructed walls or temple footprints into measured facts.
disclaimer: This is a period-aware geographic teaching scene. Existing atlas coordinates locate established terrain, archaeological zones, approximate areas, or explicitly traditional associations; they do not supply an exact First Temple footprint, a single permanent coordinate for Zion, or reconstructed ancient walls. A configured DEM shows modern measured elevation, not an ancient architectural surface.

evidenceLegend.label: Physical terrain
evidenceLegend.description: Established geographic features or measured terrain when a verified DEM is configured.

evidenceLegend.label: Known archaeology
evidenceLegend.description: Archaeological features or zones represented at the level supported by existing project records.

evidenceLegend.label: Historical inference
evidenceLegend.description: Period interpretation derived from texts and archaeology but not a directly observed feature at this exact point.

evidenceLegend.label: Tradition
evidenceLegend.description: A later or canonical association kept distinct from archaeological certainty.

evidenceLegend.label: Unknown / disputed
evidenceLegend.description: A location, footprint, boundary, or reconstruction that cannot responsibly be fixed to an exact coordinate.

evidenceLegend.label: Artistic reconstruction
evidenceLegend.description: Project-authored visualization used to evoke a period landscape; it is not measured archaeology or a recovered historical view.

periods.note: Shows the enduring terrain relationships: southeastern ridge, eastern ridge, Kidron Valley, Gihon Spring, and Temple Mount precinct. No ancient city boundary is reconstructed.

camera.note: A teaching camera chosen to show the ridge-and-valley relationship; it is not a historical viewpoint.

periods.label: Pre-monarchic
periods.note: Keeps the focus on the southeastern ridge and water source while avoiding a detailed city reconstruction unsupported by this prototype.

camera.note: Camera centers on the established southeastern-ridge archaeological zone; no pre-monarchic wall line is asserted.

periods.label: Davidic
periods.note: Highlights the captured stronghold/City of David textual association, Gihon, Kidron, and Mount of Olives while leaving disputed structures and precise urban extent unresolved.

camera.note: Centers the established southeastern ridge, not a claimed footprint of David's palace or the Jebusite stronghold.

periods.label: First Temple
periods.note: Shows the Temple Mount precinct as the traditional/historical temple location while explicitly withholding an exact First Temple footprint or reconstructed building plan.

camera.note: Frames the southeastern ridge and Temple Mount precinct together; it does not locate Solomon's temple within the platform.

periods.label: Late Iron Age
periods.note: Adds the securely located Gihon-to-Siloam water system context while keeping wall lines, population extent, and individual royal building attributions interpretive.

camera.note: Camera emphasizes the established water-system zone; it does not turn every nearby rock-cut feature into a biblical attribution.

periods.label: Persian
periods.note: Provides post-exilic Jerusalem context without drawing an exact restored wall circuit or temple plan in advance of verified period-specific spatial datasets.

camera.note: Regional Jerusalem framing only; no exact Persian-period boundary is asserted.

periods.label: Hasmonean
periods.note: Places later Second Temple Jerusalem in its topographic setting while leaving specific fortification and precinct reconstructions for a verified archaeological layer.

camera.note: Broad city teaching camera; it is not a Hasmonean wall reconstruction.

periods.label: Herodian
periods.note: Highlights the Herodian-period Jerusalem setting and Second Temple precinct without displaying an unverified building mesh or pretending the present platform is an untouched first-century surface.

camera.note: Centers the established Temple Mount/Haram al-Sharif precinct as geographic context, not an exact reconstruction of the Herodian sanctuary.

periods.label: c. 30 CE
periods.note: A Gospel-period geography view linking the Temple precinct, Kidron Valley, Mount of Olives, and Siloam without fixing debated trial, crucifixion, or burial sites in this batch.

camera.note: Teaching view across first-century Jerusalem geography; Passion candidate locations are reserved for Batch 6.

periods.label: 70 CE
periods.note: Frames Jerusalem and the Temple precinct at the end of the revolt without animating destruction or claiming a building-by-building siege reconstruction.

camera.note: Geographic context only; no siege line, legion position, or destruction footprint is asserted.

hotspots.label: Southeastern Ridge / City of David archaeological zone
hotspots.summary: The narrow ridge south of the Temple Mount preserves Jerusalem's earliest urban core; the modern archaeological label should not be confused with every biblical use of 'City of David' or 'Zion'.

whyShown.evidence: The existing atlas identifies the southeastern ridge as the archaeological zone containing Jerusalem's earliest urban core.
whyShown.inference: The scene can use the ridge to explain topography and settlement development without assigning disputed structures to named kings.
whyShown.alternatives: Biblical terms such as Zion and City of David have textual histories that are not reducible to one permanent polygon.

hotspots.label: Gihon Spring
hotspots.summary: Jerusalem's principal ancient spring and a fixed topographic anchor for understanding the southeastern ridge and water systems.

whyShown.evidence: Gihon is an established physical and archaeological feature in the existing atlas.
whyShown.inference: Its relationship to the ridge helps explain why water access mattered to Jerusalem's development; this does not identify every biblical water-system episode with a particular excavated feature.

hotspots.label: Kidron Valley
hotspots.summary: The valley immediately east of ancient Jerusalem, providing a major topographic separation between the city ridge and Mount of Olives.

whyShown.evidence: The Kidron Valley is a secure geographic feature east of Jerusalem.
whyShown.inference: A single atlas point represents a valley area for interaction; it is not a claim that biblical crossings occurred at that exact pixel.

hotspots.label: Mount of Olives ridge
hotspots.summary: The established ridge east of Jerusalem, important in David's flight and later Gospel geography.

whyShown.evidence: The Mount of Olives ridge is a securely identified geographic landmark.
whyShown.inference: The ridge coordinate does not identify an exact tree, teaching spot, route, or later shrine as the location of a biblical episode.

hotspots.label: Temple Mount / Haram al-Sharif precinct
hotspots.summary: The physical sacred precinct north of the southeastern ridge, historically associated with the First and Second Temples while the exact First Temple footprint remains archaeologically inaccessible and uncertain.

whyShown.evidence: The precinct itself is an established physical location with strong historical association to the Jerusalem temples.
whyShown.inference: Using the precinct as a scene anchor does not identify the exact First Temple footprint or reproduce a verified Herodian sanctuary plan.
whyShown.alternatives: Future reconstructions must distinguish the physical platform, period-specific expansions, textual temple references, and the uncertainty of inaccessible subsurface remains.

hotspots.label: Exact First Temple footprint: not mapped
hotspots.summary: The atlas intentionally refuses to draw an exact First Temple building footprint from the available project evidence.

whyShown.evidence: Biblical texts describe the temple, and the Temple Mount precinct is historically associated with it, but the existing project does not possess direct excavation of an exact First Temple footprint.
whyShown.inference: The hotspot is a warning attached to the precinct, not a building coordinate.
whyShown.alternatives: Any future footprint visualization must be labeled interpretive and cite the reconstruction model used.

hotspots.label: Siloam / Hezekiah's Tunnel
hotspots.summary: The established rock-cut tunnel carrying Gihon water toward the southern part of ancient Jerusalem, commonly associated with Hezekiah's preparations.

whyShown.evidence: The tunnel and inscription are archaeological realities in Jerusalem's water system.
whyShown.inference: The inscription itself does not name Hezekiah; the common association depends on archaeological and biblical context.

hotspots.label: Pool of Siloam — Second Temple period
hotspots.summary: The excavated Second Temple-period pool at the southern end of the City of David area, associated in John 9 with the healing of the man born blind.

whyShown.evidence: The existing Gospel-period atlas record identifies the excavated pool complex at this location.
whyShown.inference: The archaeology establishes the pool setting; it does not independently adjudicate the theological meaning of John 9.

hotspots.label: Moriah — canonical/traditional Jerusalem association
hotspots.summary: Genesis 22 names the land of Moriah; 2 Chronicles 3:1 later names Mount Moriah for Solomon's temple, creating the canonical basis for the Jerusalem association without turning Genesis 22 into a modern surveyed coordinate.

whyShown.evidence: The canonical link comes from reading Genesis 22 alongside 2 Chronicles 3:1.
whyShown.inference: The atlas places the Moriah association at the Temple Mount tradition while retaining its traditional coordinate role.
whyShown.alternatives: Genesis 22 itself does not provide a modern coordinate, and this scene does not claim archaeological proof of Abraham's precise location.

hotspots.label: Zion changes meaning — no single permanent pin
hotspots.summary: In 2 Samuel 5 Zion names the captured stronghold/City of David context; later biblical usage broadens toward Jerusalem and the temple. The underlying atlas record therefore intentionally has no coordinates.

whyShown.evidence: The existing atlas explicitly models Zion as a changing biblical toponym and stores no coordinate for the Zion record itself.
whyShown.inference: This hotspot is placed on the southeastern ridge only to explain the early 2 Samuel association in the active period view; it is not a coordinate assigned to Zion.
whyShown.alternatives: Later biblical and traditional uses broaden or shift the term, so the scene changes explanation rather than moving a supposed eternal Zion pin.

reconstruction.title: Jerusalem c. 30 CE — animated reconstruction
reconstruction.alt: Layered artistic reconstruction of Herodian-period Jerusalem viewed across the Kidron Valley from the Mount of Olives.
reconstruction.note: Animated artistic reconstruction. Terrain relationships and known archaeology inform the composition, but urban density, roofscape, vegetation placement, atmospheric effects, and inner-Temple appearance are illustrative.
